item.title: Sharp drops for AI stocks overwhelm markets worldwide as oil prices jump
item.description: Drops for stocks in the artificial-intelligence industry are dragging down markets worldwide on Thursday, while oil prices hit their highest levels since May because of worries about the war with Iran ...
item.dc:creator: The Associated Press
item.content:encoded: NEW YORK — The latest shudder for stocks in the artificial intelligence industry pulled markets lower worldwide on Thursday, while oil prices hit their highest levels since May on worries about the war with Iran. The S&P 500 fell 1.2 per cent for its worst day since July, while the Nasdaq composite tumbled 2.6 per cent. The weakness for tech stocks was so overwhelming that it masked strength for the rest of the U.S. market, where the majority of stocks actually rose. The Dow Jones Industrial Average added 11 points, or less than 0.1 per cent. AI-related stocks have been swinging on worries that their boom may be under threat because of how expensive it’s become to borrow money to build data centers and buy more AI chips. Concerns also remain that their prices shot too high following a yearslong frenzy, even though companies in the industry continue to report growth. Lam Research, whose equipment and services help make semiconductors, reported gains in profit and revenue for the summer that were slightly stronger than analysts expected, for example. Usually, that helps boost a stock’s price, but Lam Research’s tumbled 11.8 per cent. It gave a range for its forecast for profit this quarter whose midpoint was slightly below analysts’ expectations. Its stock also came into the day with a 52.4 per cent surge for the year so far, nearly quadruple the gain for the overall S&P 500, leaving plenty of room for potential disappointment. Other big tech stocks likewise fell following quarterly reports that included at least some encouraging nuggets. Meta Platforms, which is pushing its Muse AI agent, lost 7 per cent after reporting stronger revenue for the latest quarter than analysts expected, though its profit fell short. The company behind Facebook and Instagram also said it’s creating a new class of stock to raise money to pay for AI investments and other expenses. Tesla fell 3.1 per cent after reporting a stronger profit for the summer than analysts expected, though its revenue was weaker than forecast. The global tide against AI stocks knocked Nvidia down 4.4 per cent. Because the chip giant is the largest company on Wall Street by total value, movements for its stock carry more weight on the S&P 500 than any other, and it was the single strongest force pulling the index lower. CoreWeave, which has borrowed money to buy Nvidia’s AI chips that it rents out to customers over the cloud, has been particularly shaky in recent weeks because of worries about its debt. It dropped 10.1 per cent. The weakness for AI and other tech stocks began in Asia, where indexes are full of players in the industry. South Korea’s Kospi tumbled 3.5 per cent, Hong Kong’s Hang Seng dropped 3 per cent and Japan’s Nikkei 225 sank 2.7 per cent. Also weighing on global stock markets was a jump in oil prices. The price for a barrel of Brent crude oil leaped 4 per cent to US$113.17 after touching its highest level in five months. It’s shot up from less than US$97 at the start of the month on uncertainty about when the war with Iran will allow the global energy industry to return to normal. In Europe, France’s CAC 40 stock index fell to one of the continent’s sharpest losses with a drop of 1.4 per cent. It has fewer tech stocks than Asian or U.S. indexes, but it was hurt by another jump in yields for French government bonds. Yields have been generally climbing there because of worries about the government’s big debt load and strained budget. Violent protests across France have raised pressure on the government to increase spending, which could add further to its debt. Worries about big government debt are weighing on almost every developed economy in the world, including the United States. Such concerns, along with high inflation, signals of a still-strong U.S. economy and other factors, have pushed yields in the U.S. bond market recently to their highest levels in decades. But U.S. yields nevertheless fell sharply Thursday in a signal that investors were buying U.S. government bonds in search of something safer to own as AI stocks tumbled. The yield on the 10-year Treasury tumbled to 4.97 per cent from 5.13 per cent late Wednesday and from more than 5.30 per cent earlier this month. That’s a major move for the bond market. Thursday’s drop in yields came even as another report suggested the U.S. economy may be doing better than economists expected. It said fewer U.S. workers applied for unemployment benefits last week, which could signal that layoffs remain low across the country. That solid economy has helped U.S. companies broadly to make bigger profits, which is what propelled the U.S. stock market to a record high earlier this month despite the many worries tugging at it. Two out of every three stocks within the S&P 500 rose Thursday, only to get drowned out by the drops for more influential tech stocks. Procter & Gamble, Lockheed Martin and CSX were among the latest companies to join the list of those topping profit expectations for the summer, and gains for their stocks helped limit the market’s losses Thursday. CEO Shailesh Jejurikar said Procter & Gamble expects “geopolitical and economic challenges” to continue, but it stood by its forecasts for growth in revenue, profit and other measures for the full year. The stock price for the company behind the Crest, Olay and Oral-B brands rose 5.6 per cent. All told, the S&P 500 fell 93.74 points to 7,663.43. The Dow Jones Industrial Average added 11.89 to 52,867.98, and the Nasdaq composite tumbled 694.00 to 26,008.86. ___ Stan Choe, The Associated Press AP Business Writer Elaine Kurtenbach contributed to this report.

item.title: Tesla drops as spending pullback clouds AI, robotics ambitions
item.description: Tesla’s shares slid five per cent in premarket trading on Thursday as the EV maker’s reduced capital spending forecast raised questions about the pace of investment behind Elon Musk’s AI, robotics and ...
item.dc:creator: Reuters Staff
item.content:encoded: Tesla’s shares slid five per cent in premarket trading on Thursday as the EV maker’s reduced capital spending forecast raised questions about the pace of investment behind Elon Musk’s AI, robotics and autonomous-driving ambitions. The company on Wednesday lowered its 2026 capital spending forecast to about US$20 billion from more than $25 billion after spending far less than expected on AI and robotics in the third quarter, which led to a surprise positive free cash flow. The strong position may prove valuable as CEO Musk explores combining Tesla with the far more capital-intensive SpaceX. But “investors are likely to come away with mixed feelings,” J.P.Morgan analysts, led by Rajat Gupta, wrote in a note. “The delay helps near-term cash burn but also suggests delays in investments that matter for fruition of long-term opportunities.” Wednesday’s management commentary suggested spending will be ramped up in 2027 and 2028 as Tesla continues to fund robotaxi, Optimus, AI compute and Terafab milestones, the brokerage said. Tesla’s shares have declined about 14 per cent this year, in contrast to the Nasdaq’s roughly 15 per cent gain. The stock is about 23 per cent below its record intraday high of $498.83, reached in December 2025. Its valuation, however, remains well above peers: Tesla traded at 188.24 times its forward earnings estimates, compared with 6.58 for Ford and 5.16 for General Motors. “The risk is Tesla now enters a period of limbo while investors await news on a potential combination with SpaceX, which ... might face significant regulatory hurdles,” said Russ Mould, investment director at AJ Bell. (Reporting by Joel Jose in Bengaluru; Editing by Joyjeet Das)

item.title: Melanie Paradis: Streamlining mines is good, but Ottawa needs a plan to finance them
item.description: Political analyst and communications expert Melanie Paradis warns that the federal government’s new fast-track regulatory bill will not be enough to spark a new resources boom, unless Ottawa actively ...
item.content:encoded:
Melanie Paradis is the president of Texture Communications and has worked at the intersection of mining and politics for 20 years. There is a tendency in Ottawa to think that if you permit a mine, the capital will flow. But those working in the mining industry and on Bay Street know it isn’t that simple.

This week, Energy and Natural Resources Minister Tim Hodgson said the world is entering the “largest investment supercycle in the history of the metals and mining industry.” A supercycle refers to a long period of investment in new mines driven by significant shifts in the global economy. According to Hodgson, this supercycle is tied to increased demand for critical minerals generated by changes to the industrial strategies and economic policies of many countries. To leverage this, the federal government introduced Bill C-39 , the Building Canada Strong Act , to compress into one year a federal approvals process that routinely takes several. But while government policy decides which projects are permitted, prices decide which ones get built. When the two line up, Canada builds mines. When they don’t, no amount of legislative reform fills the gap. To actually build Canada strong, C-39 must be the first step in a countercyclical industrial strategy for mining that would accelerate viable projects today, build the infrastructure tomorrow’s mines will need, and work with allies to make strategically important minerals financeable even when markets are manipulated. Let’s start with the last time a government bet on regulatory reform. In 2012, Stephen Harper’s government overhauled federal environmental assessments to speed up resource development, just as the last commodity supercycle was ending. Mineral exploration spending in Canada fell from about $4.2 billion in 2011 to $1.6 billion in 2016. The new rules were designed to be faster, but the regulatory reform alone could not reverse the collapse in investment. The capital hurdle Today’s federal government must learn from that experience that while C-39 can make a mine permittable, it can’t attract investors to the mine with a permit alone. The reverse is also true. Government would also be wise not to spurn financeable mines with an overly narrow definition of “national interest.” Gold is a good example. According to the Scotia Growth Institute , gold now accounts for 46 per cent of the value of Canada’s 10 largest mining commodities, up from just 24 per cent three years ago. Gold projects have and will continue to advance in response to market demand, and for that reason they tend to fly under the notice of governments. But treating gold as an afterthought because it doesn’t fit the critical minerals narrative would be a mistake. A gold mine that opens in 2028 trains a workforce and builds the roads and power lines that the next critical-minerals project will be able to leverage. It also proves to investors that Canada can take a deposit from discovery to production. When prices for other commodities recover, that track record will let Canadian critical minerals projects raise capital quickly. It’s therefore in the national interest for viable mines that don’t meet the definition of “critical minerals,” like gold, to be opened. Beijing’s market chokehold Some critical minerals are not as easily financed in the current market, and many of Canada’s biggest deposits sit in feasibility purgatory despite the government’s desire to see them advance. And this is not by accident. Beijing floods the market to drive down prices, which starves Western projects of capital so they don’t get built, securing China’s grip on vital supply chains. A U.S. congressional select committee has documented this predatory pricing, and Washington is now pursuing agreements to establish a trade zone for critical minerals with tariffs and price floors to help build supply chains within allied countries. Because of ongoing trade negotiations with the U.S., Canada has not yet committed to that plan. The job of government is to invest in readiness during the lean years so that when prices align, projects are permitted, financed and ready to build. C-39 offers a tool for that. Its proposed Regions of National Interest could streamline federal approvals inside a designated mining district, for example. The time to designate those regions with provinces and Indigenous partners is now; we should build the roads and power lines that will make future mines less expensive to develop. Laying that foundation also means treating the national-interest list as a floor, not a ceiling. The projects on the list deserve the attention they’re getting, but the same speed should be available to every viable mine. And where the government invests its own money, it should strategically serve as a counterweight to market manipulation. Taken together, these steps would form the foundation of a countercyclical industrial strategy for mining to ensure we are ready for the mining supercycle, Hodgson says, is just beginning. item.title: When should you start collecting CPP and OAS?: Stan Wong
item.description: Who would turn down a 42 per cent pay raise? That is effectively the choice facing Canadians deciding when to collect their Canada Pension Plan (CPP).
item.content:encoded:
Who would turn down a 42 per cent pay raise? That is effectively the choice facing Canadians deciding when to collect their Canada Pension Plan (CPP). Waiting until 70 rather than starting at 65 increases monthly payments by 42 per cent. The catch? Five years without collecting a penny.

Clients frequently ask me whether they should begin collecting CPP as early as age 60, wait until 65 or defer until 70, and when they should start Old Age Security (OAS). Many instinctively favour taking the money early. But the better question is how these decisions fit into their overall financial plan. Do you actually need the income? Consider two retirees, both aged 65. One has a workplace pension, substantial investments, and no immediate need for additional income. Deferring CPP could strengthen financial security later. The other relies on investment withdrawals to pay everyday expenses. Collecting earlier might reduce the need to sell investments during a market downturn. The same pension rules can produce very different answers. A comprehensive financial plan can project cash flow, compare investment withdrawals, and identify the trade-offs of waiting, including forgone returns and potential taxes. Taxes can change the calculation Both CPP and OAS are taxable, but only OAS faces an income-tested recovery tax, commonly called the clawback. For the 2026 income year, the OAS clawback starts above $95,323 in individual net income, with 15 cents recovered for each additional dollar. This generally affects recoveries from July 2027 through June 2028. At a net income of $120,000, including OAS, roughly $3,700 would be recovered. For recipients aged 65 to 74, the benefit can be fully clawed back at $155,320. CPP has no comparable clawback, although receiving it can increase taxable income and, consequently, OAS repayments. The broader retirement income picture is crucial: someone retiring before mandatory withdrawals from a registered retirement income fund (RRIF) begin may benefit from drawing down savings in a registered retirement savings plan (RRSP) during lower-income years while deferring benefits. Someone expecting substantial RRIF income later might face larger OAS clawbacks even after waiting. Coordinating pension income, registered account withdrawals and income-splitting opportunities can change which starting dates are most tax-efficient. The financial reward for waiting CPP can start at 60, with payments reduced by 36 per cent relative to 65. After 65, payments increase by 0.7 per cent for each month deferred, reaching 42 per cent at 70. OAS can start at 65. Waiting increases payments by 0.6 per cent monthly, or 36 per cent at 70. Neither benefit increases further for deferral beyond 70. Someone entitled to $1,000 monthly in CPP at 65 would receive $1,420 at 70, before future inflation adjustments. The maximum monthly OAS payment for aged 65 to 74 is $762.50 in late 2026. A 36 per cent increase would lift that base payment to approximately $1,037, before indexing. Both benefits are inflation-adjusted, and OAS rises automatically another 10 per cent at 75. How long must you live to come out ahead? Delaying $1,000 monthly in CPP from 65 to 70 means forgoing $60,000, then receiving an additional $420 monthly. On a simple cumulative-payment basis, the higher benefit catches up near age 82. For OAS, the comparable break-even is around age 83, accounting for the 10 per cent increase at 75 applicable to both starting ages. Taxes, inflation, and investment returns can change these results. According to the Office of the Chief Actuary’s 32nd CPP report , a Canadian man aged 65 in 2025 is projected to live another 21.6 years, reaching approximately age 87; for women, the projection is 24.1 years, reaching approximately age 89. These averages cannot predict individual outcomes. Health, lifestyle, and family history should inform longevity assumptions. For those who live into their 90s, higher inflation-adjusted benefits may reduce pressure on portfolios later in life. Individuals eligible for the Guaranteed Income Supplement should generally not defer OAS because doing so delays access to that supplement. A total wealth planning decision There is no universally correct age to begin CPP or OAS. Spouses may benefit from different starting dates, and taking one benefit earlier while deferring the other may make sense. Before deciding, Canadians should prepare or update a comprehensive financial plan that models different scenarios for income needs, tax exposure, portfolio sustainability, and estate objectives. The goal is not simply to collect sooner or secure the largest monthly cheque. It is to make these decisions within a broader total wealth plan that supports after-tax income and lasting financial security.
